history.heading: Indigenous Brazil
paragraphs: Before Europeans arrived, the territory of Brazil was home to millions of indigenous people belonging to hundreds of groups, such as the Tupi-Guarani along the coast and many peoples in the Amazon basin. Archaeology shows that parts of the Amazon supported large, complex societies that shaped the forest and created fertile dark soils (terra preta).

history.heading: Portuguese colony
paragraphs: Pedro Álvares Cabral claimed Brazil for Portugal in 1500. The colony's first export was brazilwood, which gave the country its name. From the mid-16th century, sugar plantations in the northeast were worked by enslaved Africans; Brazil received around 4 to 5 million enslaved people, more than any other country in the Americas.

Communities of escaped slaves, called quilombos, resisted; the most famous, Palmares, lasted most of the 17th century. Gold and diamond discoveries in Minas Gerais in the 18th century shifted the colony's centre southward, and Rio de Janeiro became the capital in 1763.

history.heading: Empire and republic
paragraphs: When Napoleon invaded Portugal in 1807, the Portuguese royal court fled to Rio de Janeiro, making it the capital of the Portuguese Empire. In 1822 Prince Pedro declared Brazil's independence and became Emperor Pedro I. Under Pedro II, who reigned for nearly 50 years, Brazil became a coffee-exporting power. It was the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery, in 1888.

The monarchy was overthrown in 1889, and the republic was dominated by coffee and dairy oligarchies. Getúlio Vargas took power in 1930 and ruled for long periods, promoting industrialisation and labour laws. The capital moved to the newly built city of Brasília in 1960.

history.heading: Dictatorship and democracy
paragraphs: A military coup in 1964 began a dictatorship that lasted until 1985, combining rapid economic growth with repression. Democracy returned with a new constitution in 1988. The Real Plan of 1994 ended hyperinflation.

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of the Workers' Party, president from 2003 to 2010, oversaw a commodity boom and major reductions in poverty. A deep recession and corruption scandals followed, President Dilma Rousseff was impeached in 2016, and far-right Jair Bolsonaro was elected in 2018. Lula returned to power in 2023; a week later Bolsonaro supporters stormed government buildings in Brasília, and Bolsonaro was later convicted of plotting a coup.

culture.heading: A mixed heritage
paragraphs: Brazil is the largest Portuguese-speaking country in the world. Its people have indigenous, European, African and Asian origins; it has the largest population of African descent outside Africa and the largest Japanese community outside Japan. Brazil has the world's largest Catholic population, while evangelical Protestantism has grown rapidly, and Afro-Brazilian religions such as Candomblé are practised.

culture.heading: Music, carnival and the arts
paragraphs: Carnival, especially the samba school parades of Rio de Janeiro and the street festivities of Salvador and Recife, is world famous. Brazilian music is extraordinarily rich, including samba, bossa nova (with Antônio Carlos Jobim and João Gilberto), MPB, forró, sertanejo and funk carioca.

Capoeira, a martial art combining dance and music developed by enslaved Africans, is recognised by UNESCO. Writers include Machado de Assis, Jorge Amado and Clarice Lispector, and Oscar Niemeyer designed the modernist buildings of Brasília.

culture.heading: Food and football
paragraphs: Feijoada, a black bean and pork stew, is considered the national dish. Other favourites include churrasco (barbecue), pão de queijo (cheese bread), açaí and brigadeiros, with caipirinha as the national cocktail.

Football is a national passion. Brazil has won the FIFA World Cup a record five times and produced legends such as Pelé, Garrincha, Ronaldo and Marta. Volleyball, mixed martial arts and Formula One, with Ayrton Senna, are also popular.

politics.heading: Federal presidential republic
paragraphs: Brazil is a federal republic of 26 states and the Federal District. The president, elected directly for a four-year term with one consecutive re-election allowed, is head of state and government. The National Congress consists of the Chamber of Deputies and the Federal Senate.

Brazil has a highly fragmented party system, so presidents must build large coalitions in Congress. Politics has become strongly polarised between the left, led by Lula's Workers' Party, and the right, shaped by Bolsonaro.

politics.heading: Global role
paragraphs: Brazil is the largest country in Latin America and a leading voice of the Global South. It is a founding member of BRICS and Mercosur and a member of the G20. It hosted the COP30 climate conference in Belém in 2025. Protecting the Amazon rainforest, the world's largest tropical forest, is a central environmental and diplomatic issue.

economy.heading: An agricultural and industrial giant
paragraphs: Brazil has one of the largest economies in the world. It is the world's leading exporter of soybeans, coffee, sugar, orange juice and beef, and a major producer of iron ore and oil, especially from deep offshore fields. China is its largest trading partner.

Industry includes cars, aircraft (Embraer is a major manufacturer), steel, chemicals and food processing. Brazil is a leader in renewable energy, with most electricity from hydropower and widespread use of sugarcane ethanol in cars.

economy.heading: Challenges
paragraphs: Brazil has high income inequality, though programmes such as Bolsa Família have reduced extreme poverty. Other challenges include a complex tax system (being reformed), high interest rates, infrastructure gaps, crime and deforestation. The currency is the real.
